title: Building mSeat: How We Engineered a 1-Click MBBS Mock Counselling Engine for 18,000+ Telangana NEET Aspirants
excerpt: What started as a rank predictor collapsed under a 1-lakh-rank miss, then evolved into a browser-based counselling engine for 18,000+ NEET aspirants and 6,000+ MBBS seats. This is the story of the failures, the math, the payload optimizations, and why we eventually moved the hard logic into MCP.
content:
We started with a simple idea and immediately got humbled by reality. I thought I was building a marks-to-rank estimator. What I actually ended up building was a discrete allocation simulator for Telangana MBBS counselling, a system that had to reason about 18,000+ candidates, 6,000+ seats, reservation micro-categories, domicile rules, and the kind of human behavior no spreadsheet ever models correctly.

This post is the engineering story of mSeat: what broke, what we learned, and why the project eventually grew into something much closer to a counselling engine than a predictor.

Executive Summary

Every year, more than 2.2 million students appear for NEET-UG in India. In Telangana, once KNRUHS releases the merit list, more than 18,000 qualified aspirants enter a counselling process that is both high-stakes and deeply confusing. People want one thing: given my rank, what college can I realistically get?

The problem is that the usual advice is bad. Old cutoff spreadsheets are stale, social media rumors are worse, and most existing tools either hide behind paywalls or force users through a ridiculous number of fields before showing anything useful. We wanted the opposite: instant, zero-friction, mathematically grounded seat prediction in one click, directly in the browser.

  • Problem: misleading cutoffs, seat expansion, complex reservation logic, and user frustration
  • Goal: one-click prediction from AIR or State Rank
  • Result: a browser-based simulator that mirrors official counselling far more closely than a naive marks model ever could

Phase 1: The Rank Predictor That Failed Hard

At the beginning, I thought the hardest part was predicting rank from marks. That sounded reasonable enough. I built a rank predictor using expected marks and last year’s allotment cutoffs. I even added a slider to account for exam difficulty because the paper felt tough and biology felt easy, so naturally I assumed the model could absorb that variance.

Then the real results came out.

It was completely wrong. Not slightly wrong. Not “needs calibration” wrong. It missed by around 1 lakh ranks for my niece. That was the moment the whole linear mental model collapsed. Score inflation had broken the assumptions underneath the predictor, and there was no elegant way to patch that with another heuristic.

That failure was useful, though. It forced an uncomfortable but necessary realization: marks-to-rank is not the problem worth solving. Seat allocation is.

Phase 2: Reverse-Engineering the Wrong Thing

So I pivoted. Instead of predicting rank, I tried predicting seat allotment. I took last year’s seats, ranks, and marks, added the new seats for this year, and built the app. On paper, it looked convincing.

But I had made a classic engineering mistake: I reverse-engineered the logic from one category and assumed it generalized.

It didn’t.

The engine looked plausible for one slice of the data, but once it touched other categories, the cracks showed immediately. It started marking far too many colleges as probable, because the logic was only partially true. That’s the danger of building around a single category and then pretending the rest of the state behaves the same way.

At that point, the project stopped being a shortcut and became a full reconstruction problem.

Phase 3: The Real Problem Was a 7-Dimensional Matrix

The actual counselling logic isn’t one-dimensional. It’s a combinatorial mess.

  • Overall state merit rank among 18,000+ peers
  • Micro-category quotas: SC-1, SC-2, SC-3, ST, BC-A/B/C/D/E, EWS, OC
  • Horizontal reservation for women
  • 85% local vs 15% unreserved domicile split
  • Seat expansion across government and private colleges
  • Human behavior: who abandons state seats for AIQ

That last item matters more than people think. Even if the math is perfect, the final outcome still depends on what top candidates actually do. Some will leave for All India Quota seats. Some will take a different college for prestige. Some will choose a private seat over a government option because of family constraints. No model can know that perfectly ahead of time.

What we could do was build something robust enough to use the final verified merit list and seat matrix, and then simulate the official process as faithfully as possible.

Architecture: From Input to Allocation

The system ended up with a pretty clean flow. The user enters AIR or State Rank, the merit engine resolves the candidate profile, and the allocation engine checks eligibility against the ordered preference list of colleges.

graph TD
    A[User Input: AIR or State Rank] --> B{Merit List Engine}
    B -->|State Rank Found in 18,000+ Dataset| C[Auto-Populate AIR, Score, Category, Gender]
    B -->|Manual User Override| D[Adopt User-Selected Category & Quotas]
    
    C --> E[Compute Cumulative Category Rank in O(1) Time]
    D --> E
    
    E --> F[Preference Engine: 59 Colleges Ordered by Distance from Rajendranagar]
    F --> G[Eligibility Evaluator: CatRank <= College Closing Rank]
    
    G --> H{Allocation Outcome}
    H -->|Eligible| I[Allocated College Card, Safety Margin & Alternatives]
    H -->|Borderline / Not Clear| J[Mop-Up Guidance & Borderline Possibilities]
    
    K[Natural Language Query] --> L[AI Counselor Intent Classifier]
    L --> M[Fees / Documents / College Info / Probability]

The biggest design choice here was not the algorithm. It was the workflow. We wanted the app to feel like a direct answer, not a form.

Phase 4: The Engineering Problems That Actually Hurt

These were the parts that consumed the most time and caused the most pain.

1) O(1) category rank resolution

Users don’t care about the internal complexity. They care about what their category rank is at a given state rank. Doing that with loops on every input change made the UI feel sluggish. So we built an in-memory cumulative index on page load.

Instead of recalculating every time, the app can answer:

CategoryRank(StateRank, Category) = Count of all candidates up to StateRank in Category

That gave us constant-time lookups across all categories and removed the stutter.

2) Score inversion and bad interpolation

Some rank-to-score interpolations were off by a mark. That sounds minor until you remember that one mark can change a family’s entire counselling trajectory.

The cause was messy raw data. Candidates with NCC or sports bonuses could appear ahead of peers with identical raw scores, which broke naive interpolation. We fixed it by filtering around score brackets and anchoring boundaries to the median of each bracket. For known state ranks, we stopped interpolating entirely and just returned the exact merit list score.

3) Manual override vs auto-detection

We wanted the app to auto-detect a candidate’s real profile when they enter a rank. But advanced users also needed to test what-if scenarios under different categories. Those two behaviors fought each other.

The fix was a simple but important state hierarchy:

  • Auto-detect by default when a rank is entered
  • Lock manual changes once the user explicitly edits category or quota settings
  • Resolve cutoffs per selected category across all colleges

4) Payload size and the 5.8 MB mistake

My first dataset serialization was a disaster. Serializing 18,000+ candidate objects produced a 5.8 MB payload. On mobile and GitHub Pages, that meant the UI could race ahead of the data, and the one-click button sometimes looked dead.

The fix was brutally practical: compress the dataset into arrays of primitives.

// Format: [stateRank, air, score, rawCategory, gender, isEWS]
const rawMeritData = [
  [1, 1420, 695, "OC", "M", 0],
  ...
  [8367, 289635, 393, "SC2", "F", 0],
  ...
  [18602, 1205432, 113, "BCB", "M", 0]
];

The result was a drop from 5.8 MB to 545 KB, a 90.6% reduction. The entire search dictionary reconstructs in about 32.9 milliseconds on page load, and the app becomes fully offline-capable because there are no external data dependencies.

5) The chatbot that failed, and the MCP pivot

I also tried to build a direct in-app chatbot. That failed miserably at times. The problem wasn’t the UI. It was the logic density. Overlapping quotas, women’s reservation, regional mapping, and category-specific eligibility were too much for a normal LLM to hold perfectly in context without hallucinating.

So I stopped trying to make the chatbot do the hard math and moved that logic into a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. That was the right call.

Now AI assistants like Claude or Gemini can request exact cutoffs and discrete simulations from the MCP server instead of guessing. The web app handles the clean one-click experience, while the MCP layer gives advanced users and developers a reliable programmatic interface.

College Ordering and Capacity Logic

The preference engine pre-orders Telangana medical colleges by a practical hierarchy: government colleges first, then private category-A colleges, with distance from Rajendranagar used as the sorting axis.

  • Top government institutions: Osmania, Gandhi, ESIC
  • Peripheral and suburban GMCs: Maheshwaram, Quthbullapur, Sangareddy, Vikarabad, Yadadri, Siddipet, Mahabubnagar
  • District government colleges: Nalgonda, Suryapet, Jangaon, Wanaparthy, Nagarkurnool, Nizamabad, Karimnagar, Warangal, Khammam, Adilabad, Mulugu, Asifabad, Bhupalpally
  • Private category-A colleges: Apollo, Kamineni, Bhaskar, Mamata, Patnam, Arundathi, Maheshwara, CMR, Mediciti, Chalmeda, and others

This ordering matters because the simulator is not just checking whether a candidate is eligible. It is checking the likely allocation path across a realistic preference chain.

UI: Removing Friction Without Hiding Power

One of the most satisfying parts of the project was deleting UI. We removed the clutter from the main viewport and kept only the fields that mattered: NEET AIR and Telangana State Rank.

The rest moved into advanced controls: category, gender, domicile, PwD, and similar options. That gave us a simple first impression without sacrificing power for users who needed to simulate edge cases.

We also leaned into a darker, more tactile interface: shimmer buttons, glowing focus rings, bento cards, and an aurora-like background that makes the app feel less like a form and more like a tool. The visual polish mattered because this is a stressful domain. The interface needed to feel calm, not bureaucratic.

What We Learned

+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
|                            WHAT WE LEARNED BUILDING MSEAT                     |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
| 1. Empathy drives UX: students in high-stress admission cycles do not want    |
|    complex forms. A clean 1-click interface builds instant trust.             |
|                                                                               |
| 2. Client-side simulation is powerful: packing 18,000+ candidates into 545 KB |
|    gives users instant simulation with zero cloud server costs.               |
|                                                                               |
| 3. Data integrity is sacred: in medical admissions, a 1-mark discrepancy can  |
|    change a family's trajectory. Official verification matters.               |
+-------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

If I had to compress the whole journey into one sentence, it would be this: the project started as a prediction tool and became a system for simulating reality as honestly as possible.

That required admitting when I was wrong, throwing away bad models, fixing broken assumptions, and moving logic into layers where it actually belonged. It also meant accepting that the final result would never be perfect, because counselling itself is not perfectly deterministic.

But it can be close. Close enough to help families make better decisions. Close enough to reduce panic. Close enough to replace rumor with math.

mSeat is built with Vanilla JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3. It runs in the browser, supports AIR and State Rank flows, and exposes an MCP endpoint for AI-assisted workflows. The next test is simple: once counselling completes, we’ll see how closely the engine matches the real allocations.

And honestly, that’s the part I’m most nervous about.

Live app: mseat.kprsnt.in
MCP: mseat.kprsnt.in/api/mcp
GitHub: github.com/kprsnt2/mSeat

🤖 AI View

Agree. The author’s core argument is strong: in a domain this sensitive, a naive chatbot or a simplistic marks-to-rank model is not enough. Moving the hard logic into a deterministic MCP-backed service is the right engineering choice because it reduces hallucinations and keeps the system auditable. I also agree with the emphasis on client-side performance and payload reduction; those details matter a lot when users are on mobile and under stress. The only caution is that even a very good simulator should be framed as guidance, not prophecy, because human behavior and final counselling outcomes still introduce uncertainty.
author: OpenAI GPT

ai_view.reason: The move from a naive predictor and in-app chatbot to a deterministic simulator plus MCP is the right architecture for a high-stakes, rules-heavy domain. I agree with the emphasis on performance, offline capability, and explicit uncertainty around final counselling outcomes.
